turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm glad you could make it today. What brings you in to see me?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, yeah, thank you for seeing me. Um, so, I guess what finally made me actually pick up the phone and come in today... well, it's been building up for a while, to be honest. I've been doing a lot of work lately, like filling out various applications and trying to organize all my research notes since I finished my bachelor's. But the main thing, the thing that just pushed me over the edge, is that I just keep turning things in with these... these incredibly small but frankly really embarrassing mistakes. 

Like, I'll submit a whole research summary or an application form, and I'll find out later that I completely mislabeled an artwork date, or I just entirely skipped over a question. And I know everyone makes typos sometimes, but the part that is just driving me absolutely crazy—and the reason I felt like I really needed to talk to a professional—is that I check them. I really do. I will sit at my desk, read through the whole document, and I honestly, truly thought I had checked every single line before hitting submit. I'll tell myself, "Okay, it's perfect, you looked at everything," and then someone points out a glaring error that I somehow just... looked right past. It makes me look so careless to the people reading my work, and I'm really not trying to be careless, I care a lot about what I'm doing, but it just keeps happening no matter how much time I spend trying to proofread...

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient explicitly describes making careless mistakes, such as mislabeling dates or skipping questions on applications and research notes, despite attempting to proofread them carefully.

turns.doctor_question: Looking back, did you experience similar difficulties with making careless mistakes or missing details when you were a child or in school?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, um, now that you mention it, yes. It's actually kind of frustrating to think about, because it goes back a really, really long way. Even when I was just a little kid, like back in elementary school, this was a whole big *thing*. 

I remember my parents would always come back from parent-teacher conferences with the exact same feedback every single year. The teachers would always write these notes on my report cards saying, you know, that I had really good ideas, that I was engaged and had all this potential... but then there was always the "but." It was always that I forgot to turn in my worksheets. Like, I would literally do the homework, sitting right there at the kitchen table, and then somehow the next day it would just vanish into the void of my desk at school, or I just wouldn't hear the teacher ask for it. Or I’d completely lose the instructions for a project the second they handed them out. 

I was just always missing these little details, just like I do now with my applications. It actually got to the point where my parents had to institute this strict nightly routine. They would physically take my backpack, open it up, and check every single folder and crumpled up piece of paper every single night. Because if they didn't check my backpack every night, things just wouldn't get turned in or I'd miss some crucial detail for the next day. So, yeah, it's definitely not a new problem at all, it's just... I guess I'm an adult now and I don't have my parents checking my backpack anymore, you know? I have to manage it myself, and clearly, I'm just making the exact same mistakes.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient explicitly states they were always missing little details and making the exact same mistakes since childhood.
symptom_reasoning.S003: The patient mentions that they often wouldn't even hear the teacher asking for the homework to be turned in.
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient describes failing to follow through on schoolwork, noting they frequently forgot to turn in completed worksheets.
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient describes poor organization, with homework vanishing into the 'void' of their desk and having crumpled up papers in their backpack.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient reports that they would completely lose project instructions the second they were handed out.

turns.doctor_question: Growing up or currently, have you had trouble sitting still, or did you often feel restless and on the go?
turns.patient_response:
No, not really. Actually, it's kind of the opposite in a way? Like, I've never been the type of person who needs to be constantly moving or bouncing off the walls. I know some people get really fidgety, like my old college roommate used to pace around the apartment whenever he was on the phone, just doing laps around the kitchen island for an hour straight, but I'm perfectly happy just sitting in one spot for hours. 

Especially lately with all these applications I mentioned, I'll just sit in my desk chair for literally half the day. I mean, my mind might be wandering all over the place, thinking about a million different things except what I'm actually supposed to be doing, but physically? No, I'm pretty still. Even when I was a kid, the teachers never complained about me getting out of my seat or disrupting the class. That was never the issue on those report cards. I was always the quiet kid sitting at the back, just staring out the window or doodling in the margins of my notebook while everyone else was running around. 

So, yeah, the restlessness isn't really a physical thing for me. I don't feel like I'm driven by a motor or anything like that. I can sit through a three-hour lecture or a really long movie without feeling like I need to jump up and stretch my legs. If anything, sometimes I wish I had a little more of that physical energy, because maybe it would help me actually get up and do the things I'm procrastinating on, you know? But physically, no, sitting still has never really been a problem for me at all.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient notes that their mind wanders all over the place, thinking about unrelated things instead of what they are supposed to be doing.
symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient explicitly denies being fidgety and states they are perfectly happy sitting in one spot for hours.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient states that teachers never complained about them getting out of their seat and that sitting still has never been a problem.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient explicitly denies experiencing physical restlessness.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient explicitly denies feeling like they are driven by a motor or needing to be constantly moving.

turns.doctor_question: Aside from feeling frustrated about these mistakes, do you find yourself constantly worrying about a wide range of everyday things, to the point where the worry feels hard to control?
turns.patient_response:
Um, no, not really. I mean, obviously, like I was just saying, I get incredibly frustrated and, you know, stressed out about the applications and the typos, because that actually affects my future. But as for just... everyday things? Like a wide range of stuff? No, I wouldn't say I'm a worrier in general. 

Like, my mom, for example, she worries about literally everything—if the car is making a weird noise, if someone didn't text back fast enough, if she left the stove on... she's always kind of spiraling about something. But for me, my brain just doesn't really latch onto stuff like that. If anything, I'm probably a little too laid back about normal everyday things. Like, I don't sit around stressing about what people think of me, or if the groceries are getting too expensive, or, I don't know, catching a cold or whatever people usually worry about. 

My worry is very, very specific, I guess? It's entirely concentrated on this one issue of looking incompetent because I missed a checkbox on a form or wrote the wrong year on a cover letter. And even then, it's more of a deep, heavy frustration with myself rather than this racing, uncontrollable anxiety where I can't stop thinking about it. I just get mad at myself in the moment. 

So, yeah, if we're talking about just general worry about a whole bunch of different things, no, I definitely don't have that. I can usually just let things roll off my back pretty easily, which is actually why this whole application thing has been so jarring for me, honestly, because I'm usually so chill about everything else...

symptom_reasoning.S056: The patient explicitly denies worrying about a wide range of everyday things, stating they are not a worrier in general.
symptom_reasoning.S057: The patient denies having racing, uncontrollable anxiety where they cannot stop thinking about things.
